source_text: Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἑαυτῷ λαβὼν, ὡς ἄρα θεὸν νομίζουσι τὸν οὐρανὸν Ἰουδαῖοι, τούτῳ ὡς ἄτοπον ἐπιφέρει, ἐγκαλῶν τοῖς προσκυνοῦσι μὲν τὸν οὐρανὸν οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν ἥλιον καὶ τὴν σελήνην καὶ τοὺς ἀστέρας, ὅτι τοῦτο ποιοῦ σιν Ἰουδαῖοι ὡς ἐνδεχόμενον τὸ μὲν ὅλον εἶναι (θεὸν) , τὰ μέρη δ᾿ αὐτοῦ μὴ θεῖα· καὶ ὅλον μὲν ἔοικε λέγειν τὸν οὐρανὸν μέρη δ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἥλιον καὶ σελήνην καὶ ἀστέρας. οὐ λέγουσι μὲν οὖν σαφῶς οὔτε Ἰουδαῖοι οὔτε Χριστιανοὶ τὸν οὐρανὸν θεόν. ἀλλὰ δεδόσθω κατ᾿ αὐτὸν λέγεσθαι ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων θεὸν εἶναι τὸν οὐρανὸν, ἔστω δὲ καὶ μέρη τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἥλιος καὶ σελήνη καὶ ἀστέρες (ὅπερ οὐ πάντως ἐστὶν ἀληθὲς. οὐδὲ γὰρ τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς ζῷα καὶ φυτὰ μέρη γῆς)· πόθεν δὴ καὶ καθ᾿ Ἕλληνας ἀληθὲς ὅτι, ἐὰν ὅλον τι θεὸς ᾖ, ἤδη καὶ τὰ μέρη αὐτοῦ ἐστι θεῖα; σαφῶς δὴ τὸν ὅλον κόσμον λέγουσιν εἶναι θεὸν, Στωϊκοὶ μὲν τὸν πρῶτον οἱ δ᾿ ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος τὸν δεύτερον τινὲς δ᾿ αὐτῶν τὸν τρίτον. ἆρ᾿ οὖν κατὰ τοὺς τοιούτους. ἐπεὶ τὸ ὅλον ὁ κόσμος θεός ἐστιν, ἤδη καὶ τὰ μέρη αὐτοῦ θεῖα· ὡς εἶναι θεῖα οὐ μόνον ἀνθρώπους ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα τὰ ἄλογα ζῷα. μέρη ὄντα τοῦ κόσμου, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις καὶ τὰ φυτά; εἰ δὲ μέρη τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τὰ ὄρη καὶ οἱ ποταμοὶ καὶ αἱ θάλασσαι, ἆρ᾿ ἐπεὶ ὅλος ὁ κόσμος θεός ἐστιν, ἤδη καὶ οἱ ποταμοὶ καὶ αἱ θάλασσαι θεοί εἰσιν; ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τοῦτο φήσουσιν Ἕλληνες· τοὺς δ᾿ ἐπιστατοῦντας εἰ ἄρα δαίμονας (ἢ θεοὺς, ὡς ἐκεῖνοι ὀνομάζουσι) ποταμοῖς καὶ θαλάσσαις, τούτους ἂν λέγοιεν θεούς· καὶ τὸ καθολικὸν Κέλσου γίνεται καὶ καθ᾿ Ἕλληνας, τοὺς τὴν πρόνοιαν εἰσάγοντας. ψεῦδος, ὅτι ἐάν τι ὅλον ᾖ θεὸς. πάντως τὰ μέρη τούτου ἐστὶ θεῖα. ἀκολουθεῖ δὲ τῷ Κέλσου λόγῳ. ἐὰν θεὸς ᾖ ὁ κόσμος, πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ εἶναι θεῖα, μέρη ὄντα τοῦ κόσμου. καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο θεῖα ἔσται ζῷα μυῖαι καὶ σκνίφες καὶ σκώληκες καὶ πᾶν τὸ τῶν ὄφεων εἶδος ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τῶν ὀρνέων καὶ τὸ τῶν ἰχθύων· ἅπερ οὐδ᾿ οἱ λέγοντες θεὸν εἶναι τὸν κόσμον φήσουσιν. οἱ (δὲ) κατὰ τὸν τοῦ Μωϋσέως νόμον βιοῦντες Ἰουδαῖοι, κἂν μηδὲν εἰδῶσιν ἐκδέχεσθαι κεκρυμμένως εἰρημένον τοῦ νόμου βούλημα καὶ ἀπόῤῥητόν τι ἐμφαῖνον, οὔτε τὸν οὐρανὸν φήσουσιν εἶναι θεὸν οὔτε τοὺς ἀγγέλους.
thought_title: A divine whole does not make its parts divine
pass_a_gloss: But also taking (λαβών) it to himself (ἑαυτῷ), that the Jews after all (ἄρα) consider (νομίζουσι) heaven (οὐρανός) a god (θεός), he brings on (ἐπιφέρει) to this as absurd (ἄτοπον), accusing (ἐγκαλῶν) those who worship (προσκυνοῦσι) heaven but not also the sun, moon and stars, that the Jews do this as though it were possible (ἐνδεχόμενον) for the whole (ὅλον) to be [a god] (editorial supplement) but its parts (μέρη) not divine (θεῖα); and by whole he seems to mean heaven, by its parts sun, moon and stars. Now (μὲν οὖν) neither Jews nor Christians say clearly/plainly (σαφῶς) that heaven is a god. But let it be granted (δεδόσθω) according to him (κατ᾿ αὐτόν) that it is said by Jews that heaven is a god; let also sun, moon and stars be parts of heaven (which is not altogether/necessarily true, οὐ πάντως ἀληθές; for neither are the animals (ζῷα) and plants (φυτά) on earth parts of earth); whence (πόθεν) is it true even according to the Greeks that, if some whole is a god, already (ἤδη) its parts also are divine? Clearly (σαφῶς) they say the whole world (κόσμος) is a god: the Stoics the first, those from Plato (οἱ ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος) the second, some of them the third. Is it then (ἆρ᾿ οὖν) according to such men, since the whole, the world, is a god, that already its parts also are divine, so that divine are not only humans but also all irrational animals (ἄλογα ζῷα), being parts of the world, and besides these also the plants? And if mountains and rivers and seas are parts of the world, is it, since the whole world is a god, that rivers and seas are gods? But not even this will the Greeks say; but those presiding (ἐπιστατοῦντας) over rivers and seas, whatever demons (εἰ ἄρα δαίμονας) (or gods, as those name them), these they would call gods. And Celsus's universal statement (τὸ καθολικόν) becomes, even according to Greeks who introduce providence (πρόνοια), a falsehood (ψεῦδος): that if some whole is a god, by all means (πάντως) its parts are divine. It follows (ἀκολουθεῖ) from Celsus's argument (λόγῳ) that if the world is a god, all things in it are divine, being parts of the world; and accordingly divine animals will be flies (μυῖαι), gnats (σκνίφες), worms (σκώληκες) and every kind (εἶδος) of snakes, but also that of birds and of fishes; which not even those who say the world is a god will say. But the Jews living according to the law of Moses, even if they know nothing (μηδὲν εἰδῶσιν) of how to take in (ἐκδέχεσθαι) the intention (βούλημα) of the law spoken in hidden fashion (κεκρυμμένως) and showing forth (ἐμφαῖνον) something secret (ἀπόρρητον), will say neither heaven is a god nor the angels.

pass_b_english: Celsus also assumes, on his own account, that the Jews regard heaven as a god, and he adds to this something he presents as absurd. He accuses those who worship heaven but not also the sun, the moon and the stars, saying that the Jews do this “as if it were possible for the whole to be a god while its parts are not divine.” By the whole he seems to mean heaven, and by its parts the sun, the moon and the stars.

Now neither Jews nor Christians plainly say that heaven is a god. But let it be granted, on his terms, that the Jews say heaven is a god, and let the sun, the moon and the stars also be parts of heaven (which is not necessarily true, for the animals and plants on earth are not parts of the earth either). On what ground is it true, even by the Greeks’ own account, that if some whole is a god, its parts are thereby divine as well? The Greeks plainly say that the whole world is a god: the Stoics say it is the first god, the followers of Plato the second, and some of them the third. Do such men hold, then, that since the world as a whole is a god, its parts too are thereby divine, so that not only human beings but also all the irrational animals are divine, being parts of the world, and the plants as well? And if the mountains, the rivers and the seas are parts of the world, are the rivers and the seas therefore gods because the whole world is a god? But the Greeks will not say this either. Rather, it is the demons (or gods, as they name them) that preside over rivers and seas, if there are any, that they would call gods.

And so Celsus’s general rule proves false even by the account of those Greeks who bring in providence: the rule that if some whole is a god, its parts are necessarily divine. It follows from Celsus’s argument that if the world is a god, everything in it is divine, being a part of the world. On that reasoning, flies, gnats, worms and every kind of snake, and of birds and fishes too, will be divine living beings; and not even those who say that the world is a god will say that. But the Jews who live by the law of Moses, even if they do not know at all how to understand the meaning of the law, which is expressed in a hidden way and points to something secret, will say neither that heaven is a god nor that the angels are.
notes: Celsus's phrase from 5.6 (ὡς ἐνδεχόμενον τὸ μὲν ὅλον εἶναι θεόν, τὰ μέρη δ᾿ αὐτοῦ μὴ θεῖα) is set in quotation marks, in the same English used for Celsus's quotation in 5.6; the rest of the opening is Origen's report of Celsus's view. ἑαυτῷ λαβών rendered 'assumes, on his own account'; τούτῳ ὡς ἄτοπον ἐπιφέρει 'adds to this something he presents as absurd'. '(θεόν)' is an editorial supplement in the staged text, adopted from 5.6. θεός here is the pagan philosophical notion of a cosmic god, so rendered lowercase 'a god' throughout (not the God of Scripture). σαφῶς in 'οὐ λέγουσι μὲν οὖν σαφῶς' rendered 'plainly'; it qualifies the saying (they do not plainly say it), not an assertion that it is clear, and it answers the later σαφῶς of the Greeks who 'plainly say' the world is a god. Stoics/Platonists: 'the first god ... the second ... some of them the third' follows the Greek exactly; τινὲς δ᾿ αὐτῶν most naturally means some of the Platonists, left as 'some of them'. ἤδη ('already', i.e. by that fact) rendered 'thereby'; πάντως 'necessarily' in both places. δαίμονας rendered 'demons' (consistent with the rest of this translation), with Origen's own gloss 'or gods, as they name them'; εἰ ἄρα rendered 'if there are any'. The staged text has stray full stops before ψεῦδος and πάντως and after ἆρ᾿ οὖν κατὰ τοὺς τοιούτους; punctuation regularised by sense. No Scripture quoted.
